title: Deuxième partie : variations sur l'équation des lacets [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois…, pages 293 à 650, dont table des matières] : notes et copies de notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: Grothendieck works in GL2 (or a similar group of 2x2 matrices) with fixed elements ρ and σ, the auxiliary element λ0 and the auxiliary relations (49), (57) and (60 bis) from earlier pages. N0 and N1 are nilpotent matrices (Ni² = 0). The groups L_i = {ε_i(λ) = 1 + λN_i | λ in G_a} are additive one-parameter unipotent subgroups. B̃_i is their normalizer, written on the next page as {v : v N_i v⁻¹ = det(v)·N_i}, a Borel-like group.

Goal (stated on the previous page): for any section u of B̃0 put ξ = [u,ρ] and η = [u,σ]. Show that ξ = η·ε1(μ−1) with μ = det u, which is relation (64). Then (u ↦ (ξ, η, μ)) maps B̃0 into the set H_{ρ,σ} of solutions of the system (33)–(35) of the 'équation des lacets'. The previous page checked the case u in L0 (μ = 1).

This page, general case:
(i) Since ρ N0 ρ⁻¹ = σ N0 σ⁻¹ = N1, both ρ and σ conjugate L0 onto L1, hence B̃0 onto B̃1.
(ii) Write (64) as uρu⁻¹ρ⁻¹ = uσu⁻¹σ⁻¹ ε1(μ−1). Cancel u on the left: ρu⁻¹ρ⁻¹ = σu⁻¹σ⁻¹ ε1(μ−1). Replace u by u⁻¹ (so μ becomes 1/μ): (1) ρuρ⁻¹ = σuσ⁻¹ ε1(1/μ − 1).
(iii) Put λ = ρσ⁻¹ and v = σuσ⁻¹, which lies in B̃1 with det v = μ. Since ρuρ⁻¹ = int(λ)(v), (1) becomes (**) int(λ)(v) = v·ε1(1/μ − 1).
(iv) By (60 bis), int λ = int ε1, where ε1 = ε1(1) = 1 + N1. So the identity to prove is int(ε1)(v) = v·ε1(1/μ − 1) for all v in B̃1.
(v) The next page finishes. The identity is equivalent to (1+N1)v = v(1 + (1/μ)N1), using N1² = 0. That is N1 v = μ⁻¹ v N1, i.e. v N1 v⁻¹ = μN1, which is exactly the definition of B̃1.

So the map (66), B̃0 → H_{ρ,σ}, u ↦ ([u,ρ],[u,σ],det u), is well defined. It produces 'inner' or 'trivial' solutions of the loop equations by conjugating with the normalizer of the unipotent subgroup (a coboundary-type construction). Grothendieck then asks whether it is an isomorphism; injectivity amounts to T_ρ ∩ B̃0 = {1}.
errors: Notational clash: λ denotes both the G_a parameter and the group element ρσ⁻¹ (underlined to distinguish it). This causes no logical error.
The transcription's 'δ0(λ)' must be ε0(λ) = 1 + λN0.
The page cites '(69)', but the formula being rewritten is (64) from the previous page; it is probably a misreading or a slip.

Step (iv) relies on (60 bis) (int(ρσ⁻¹) = int(ε1)), which is not visible here; if that holds, the argument is complete and correct. Implicit hypotheses: N1² = 0, and B̃1 is defined by v N1 v⁻¹ = det(v) N1 (not by the bare normalizer condition). Both are used and are consistent with the next page.

ideas.what: The one-parameter unipotent subgroups L_i = 1 + G_a·N_i and their twisted normalizers B̃_i = {v : vN_iv⁻¹ = det(v)N_i}, transported into each other by conjugation by ρ and σ
ideas.modern_name: Borel subgroup / normalizer of a unipotent radical (stabilizer of a cusp)

ideas.what: Producing solutions (ξ, η, μ) of the loop-equation system by commutators with elements of B̃0: u ↦ ([u,ρ],[u,σ],det u)
ideas.modern_name: coboundary / inner-type solutions of a non-abelian cocycle-like system (analogue of the 'trivial' elements of GT-type equations)
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure; the general idea resembles the treatment of GT-type relations in Drinfeld/Ihara-style work, but this specific map is not standard

ideas.what: Reduction of the key identity to the defining relation of B̃1 using N1² = 0 and int(ρσ⁻¹) = int(1+N1)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine verification step: an elementary 2x2 matrix computation checking that commutators with Borel-type normalizer elements give solutions of the loop equations. The only mildly interesting point is the map (66) and the question of whether it is an isomorphism, raised on the next page; nothing here appears to be a missed result.
transcription_corrections: 'le sous-groupe [?] à 1 paramètre additif': the word is 'sous-groupe', and the bracket is not needed.
'(défini comme normalisateur [?] de L1, ou de N1, comme B̃0 normalisateur [?] de L0)': 'normalisateur' is the plausible reading in both places.
'La formule (69)' is probably '(64)', the relation established on the previous page.
The first displayed formula is ρu⁻¹ρ⁻¹ = σu⁻¹σ⁻¹ ε1(μ−1); the struck-out 'ρ⁻¹σ' above it is a crossed-out false start.
The margin note reads 'pour v dans B̃1 et μ = det v'.
